tips.title: After a negative, everything becomes de
tips.body: *un*, *une* **and** *des* all collapse to **de**: *il n'y a pas de cinéma / de piscine / de magasins*. This makes the negative **easier** than the positive, because you no longer need to know the gender.

tips.title: Il y a never changes
tips.body: It means *there is* **and** *there are*, so it never has to agree with what follows. *Il y a un parc* and *il y a des magasins* use exactly the same two words — one of the few structures in French with nothing to get wrong.

tips.title: On peut unlocks every verb you know
tips.body: *On peut* + the **infinitive** means *you can*, and the verb is never conjugated. *On peut aller / faire / visiter / manger…* — every verb in your vocabulary becomes usable without a single ending to work out.

tips.title: An opinion needs a reason
tips.body: *J'aime ma ville* on its own scores little. *J'aime ma ville **parce que** c'est tranquille* scores properly. One adjective with a reason beats four adjectives without one, every time.

tips.title: Two sentences, three timeframes
tips.body: *Avant, il y **avait** un cinéma* (imperfect) and *on **va** construire une piscine* (near future), dropped into a present-tense description, demonstrate three timeframes — worth more than another list of buildings.

steps.title: Il y a, il n'y a pas
steps.body:
Almost everything you say about a town is built on two phrases.

**Il y a** — *there is* or *there are*. One phrase for both, so it never has to agree:

- *Il y a **un** cinéma.* — There is a cinema.
- *Il y a **des** magasins.* — There are shops.

**Il n'y a pas de** — *there isn't* or *there aren't*. And here is the rule that carries the marks:

$$\textbf{After a negative, un, une and des all become de.}$$

- *Il y a **un** cinéma* → *Il n'y a pas **de** cinéma.*
- *Il y a **une** piscine* → *Il n'y a pas **de** piscine.*
- *Il y a **des** magasins* → *Il n'y a pas **de** magasins.*

All three collapse to the same word. So you never have to decide whether the missing thing is masculine, feminine or plural — which makes the negative **easier** than the positive, not harder.

Before a vowel, *de* becomes ***d'***: *Il n'y a pas **d'**hôpital.*

steps.title: Décrire sa ville
steps.body:
To describe where you live you need three things: **what it is**, **where it is**, and **what is in it**.

**What it is.** *J'habite dans* **une grande ville** (a city) / **une petite ville** (a town) / **un village** / **à la campagne** (in the countryside) / **au bord de la mer** (by the sea).

**Where it is.** *dans le nord / le sud / l'est / l'ouest de l'Angleterre* — in the north, south, east or west of England. Note *dans **le** nord*, with the definite article.

**What is in it.** *Il y a…* and *Il n'y a pas de…* from the last step.

And then the thing that lifts an answer: **an opinion with a reason**.

- *J'aime habiter ici **parce qu'**il y a beaucoup à faire.* — I like living here because there's a lot to do.
- *Je n'aime pas beaucoup ma ville **car** c'est trop calme.* — I don't much like my town as it's too quiet.

*Parce que* and *car* both mean *because*. *Parce que* is the safe one to use everywhere.

A useful pattern for a fuller answer: **what it is → what there is → what there isn't → an opinion with a reason.** Four short sentences make a complete description, and each is easy on its own.

steps.title: On peut : ce qu'on peut faire
steps.body:
**On peut** + an infinitive means *you can* or *one can*, and it is the most efficient structure in this topic: one phrase, then any verb you like in its dictionary form.

- *On peut **aller** au cinéma.* — You can go to the cinema.
- *On peut **faire** du shopping.* — You can go shopping.
- *On peut **visiter** le musée.* — You can visit the museum.

The verb after *on peut* is **never** conjugated. That is the whole rule, and it means every verb you know becomes usable immediately.

Its negative works the same way: *On **ne** peut **pas** aller au théâtre.*

**Where you go: au, à la, aux.** *À* combines with the definite article, and the form depends on the noun:

- *au* before a masculine noun — *au cinéma*, *au parc*
- *à la* before a feminine noun — *à la piscine*, *à la gare*
- *à l'* before a vowel — *à l'église*
- *aux* before a plural — *aux magasins*

This is the same pattern as *du / de la / des*, one row down the same table, which is why learning either helps with the other.

steps.title: Donner son opinion
steps.body:
An opinion without a reason scores far less than one with. The structure is always the same: **opinion + *parce que* + reason**.

**Opinions**

- *J'aime…* / *J'adore…* — I like / I love
- *Je n'aime pas…* / *Je déteste…* — I don't like / I hate
- *Je préfère…* — I prefer
- *À mon avis…* — In my opinion

**Reasons: useful adjectives**

- *tranquille* — quiet, peaceful (positive)
- *calme* — calm, quiet
- *animé* — lively
- *ennuyeux* — boring
- *propre* / *sale* — clean / dirty
- *bruyant* — noisy

Notice that *tranquille* and *ennuyeux* can describe the **same** town — one approving, one not. Choosing the adjective that matches your opinion is what makes the sentence hang together.

**Two things that lift an answer.**

**Say both sides.** *J'aime ma ville parce que c'est tranquille, **par contre** il n'y a pas grand-chose à faire.* A balanced view reads as a real opinion rather than a recited phrase.

**Use a different tense.** *Avant, il y avait un cinéma, mais il a fermé.* — There used to be a cinema, but it closed. One imperfect and one perfect in a present-tense answer shows range, and range is marked.

steps.title: Aller plus loin : le piège de l'article
steps.body:
**The mistake this topic is built around.** *Il n'y a pas **des** magasins* is wrong, and it is wrong for a reason worth understanding rather than memorising.

After a negative, French does not say *not some shops* — it says *not **of** shops*. So **un, une and des all become de**. The idea *some* disappears entirely, because you are talking about an absence, and an absence has no quantity.

That also explains the exception. The **definite** article does **not** change:

- *Je n'aime pas **le** cinéma.* — I don't like the cinema (as a thing).
- *Il n'y a pas **de** cinéma.* — There isn't a cinema.

The first is about a specific, known thing; the second is about a quantity of nothing. Only the indefinite and partitive articles collapse.

One genuine exception: after **être**, the article does **not** change — *Ce n'est pas **un** problème*, not *pas de problème* in that structure. You are unlikely to need it here, but if you meet *ce n'est pas un…* and wonder why it survived, that is why.

**Getting beyond the present tense.** Almost every student describes their town entirely in the present. Two sentences change that, and both are easy:

- *Avant, il y avait un cinéma.* — the **imperfect** of *il y a*, for what used to be.
- *L'année prochaine, on va construire une nouvelle piscine.* — the **near future**, for what is going to happen.

Those two sentences, dropped into a present-tense description, demonstrate three timeframes. That is worth more than another list of buildings.

**Say what is *not* there.** A description that only lists what exists reads like a catalogue. *Il n'y a pas de cinéma, donc on doit aller en ville* — there's no cinema, so you have to go into town — shows a consequence, uses the negative article correctly, and sounds like someone describing their actual life.

**Avoid the adjective pile.** *Ma ville est jolie, tranquille, propre et calme* says less than *Ma ville est tranquille, parce qu'il n'y a pas beaucoup de circulation.* One adjective with a reason beats four without.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- **Il y a** means *there is* **and** *there are* — it never changes.
- **Il n'y a pas de** means *there isn't* and *there aren't*.
- After a negative, **un, une and des all become de** — so gender and number stop mattering.
- Before a vowel, *de* becomes **d'**: *il n'y a pas d'hôpital*.
- The **definite** article does **not** change: *je n'aime pas le cinéma*.
- Describe a town in four sentences: **what it is → what there is → what there isn't → an opinion with a reason**.
- *J'habite dans une petite ville **dans le** nord de l'Angleterre* — with the article after *dans*.
- **On peut + infinitive** means *you can*, and the verb is **never conjugated**.
- **au** (masculine), **à la** (feminine), **à l'** (vowel), **aux** (plural).
- An opinion needs a **reason**: *parce que* or *car*.
- Use **par contre** to give the other side — a balanced view reads as a real opinion.
- Reach beyond the present: *avant, il y avait…* (imperfect) and *on va construire…* (near future).
- One adjective **with a reason** beats four without.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The four required sentences, then two that lift it.**

*J'habite dans une petite ville **dans le** nord de l'Angleterre.* — where, with the article after *dans*.

*Il y a un parc, des magasins et une bibliothèque.* — what there is.

*Par contre, il n'y a pas **de** cinéma et il n'y a pas **de** piscine.* — what there isn't. **De**, not *un* or *une* — the rule this topic turns on.

*J'aime habiter ici **parce que** c'est tranquille, **mais** il n'y a pas grand-chose à faire pour les jeunes.* — an opinion, a reason, **and both sides**.

**The two that raise the grade:**

*Avant, il y **avait** un cinéma, mais il **a fermé**.* — imperfect **and** perfect.

*L'année prochaine, on **va construire** un centre sportif.* — near future.

Those two sentences give three timeframes in what is otherwise a present-tense answer, and that is worth more than another list of buildings.

questions.prompt: Explique la règle : pourquoi dit-on *il n'y a pas de cinéma* et non *il n'y a pas un cinéma* ? Donne trois exemples.
questions.skill: il y a and the negative
questions.solution: En français, après une négation, les articles indéfinis un et une et l'article partitif des deviennent tous de. On ne dit donc pas il n'y a pas un cinéma mais il n'y a pas de cinéma. La raison est qu'on parle d'une absence, et une absence n'a pas de quantité, donc l'idée de un ou de quelques disparaît. Trois exemples montrent que la règle est la même quel que soit le genre ou le nombre : il y a un parc devient il n'y a pas de parc, il y a une piscine devient il n'y a pas de piscine, et il y a des magasins devient il n'y a pas de magasins. Cela rend en fait le négatif plus facile que le positif, parce qu'on n'a plus besoin de savoir si le nom est masculin, féminin ou pluriel. Il faut noter que devant une voyelle de devient d', comme dans il n'y a pas d'hôpital. Il faut noter aussi que l'article défini ne change pas : on dit je n'aime pas le cinéma, parce qu'il s'agit d'une chose précise et non d'une quantité.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The rule.** After a negative, **un**, **une** and **des** all become **de**.

**Why.** You are describing an **absence**, and an absence has no quantity — so the idea of *a* or *some* disappears. French says *not **of** cinema* rather than *not **a** cinema*.

**Three examples**, covering all three cases:

- *Il y a **un** parc* → *Il n'y a pas **de** parc.*
- *Il y a **une** piscine* → *Il n'y a pas **de** piscine.*
- *Il y a **des** magasins* → *Il n'y a pas **de** magasins.*

Because all three collapse to the same word, the **negative is easier than the positive**: you no longer need to know the gender or number.

**Two details.**

- Before a vowel, *de* becomes **d'**: *il n'y a pas **d'**hôpital*.
- The **definite** article does **not** change: *je n'aime pas **le** cinéma* — a specific known thing, not a quantity.

examTechnique.body:
Build a description in four sentences: what it is, what there is, what there isn't, and an opinion with a reason.

Check the article after every negative. Un, une and des all become de, and d' before a vowel.

Use on peut and an infinitive to say what one can do, rather than conjugating a new verb.

Give both sides with par contre or mais. A balanced view reads as a real opinion.

Add one past and one future sentence to reach three timeframes without adding difficulty.

Prefer one adjective with a reason to a list of adjectives without one.
examinerErrors: Writing il n'y a pas des magasins instead of pas de magasins.
Writing il n'y a pas un cinéma instead of pas de cinéma.
Forgetting that de becomes d' before a vowel.
Changing the definite article after a negative, as in je n'aime pas de cinéma.
Conjugating the verb after on peut.
Using au with a feminine noun, as in au piscine.
Giving an opinion with no reason.

It uses *on peut* and an infinitive to say a great deal with very little grammar. It gives an opinion with a reason and then the other side, so the description reads as a view rather than a recitation. And it reaches a past and a future timeframe in two easy sentences, which demonstrates more range than any number of extra buildings.
